title: Development
summary: Development is a broad idea whose meaning changes with the person and the situation, so different people can have different and even conflicting goals. The chapter builds the tools needed to judge development objectively: per capita income, health, education and public facilities. Countries and states are compared through average income, but averages hide unequal distribution, so indicators like the infant mortality rate, literacy rate, net attendance ratio and Body Mass Index give a fuller picture. The classic Kerala versus Haryana comparison shows that money alone cannot buy health or learning, because Kerala spends better on public facilities despite a lower income. The Human Development Report ranks countries on health, education and income together, and places India below Sri Lanka and even smaller neighbours. Finally, development must be sustainable: renewable resources like groundwater must not be used faster than they recharge, and non renewable resources like crude oil must be conserved so that future generations are not cheated of their share.

sections.heading: What Development Means to Different People
sections.para: Development has no single definition because life situations differ from person to person, and each person visualises improvement in her own way. For a landless rural labourer, development may mean daily employment, better wages and schooling for children, while for an urban unemployed youth it may mean more job opportunities in cities. An adivasi displaced by a dam may see the same project as destruction, although an industrialist sees it as cheap electricity for factories. This is why development goals can be different and even conflicting, and a national plan must balance many such claims. People also desire things besides income: equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others, which are as vital as money. Hence a good development goal combines more income with better quality of life, and any comparison of development must ask whose wellbeing is improving and who is being left behind.
points: Development promises growth and progress, but its meaning changes with the situation and needs of each person.
A landless labourer dreams of regular work and better wages, while a prosperous urban family may want cleaner air and better schools.
Development for one group may be destructive for another, as when a dam brings electricity to cities but displaces adivasi villages.
An adivasi family losing its land sees the same project very differently from an industrialist who wants cheap power for factories.
People seek mixed goals: more income together with freedom, security, respect and equal treatment in society.
Non material goals like a safe environment, job security and support of friends and family cannot be bought with money.
Since goals often conflict, national development requires balancing the claims of different groups rather than pleasing one section alone.
For exam writing, always quote two contrasting examples, one of a poor worker and one of a rich producer.

keyTerms.meaning: An aim a person considers improvement in life, such as more income, freedom, security or respect
Goals in which what is development for one person becomes destruction for another, as with a dam and displaced people
A goal not measured in money, such as respect, equal treatment, job security or a safe environment
The work, income and family circumstances that shape what a person wants from development
The combination of material and non material aims that people hold at the same time
Overall good living including income, health, education, security and dignity

sections.trick: DREAM: Dam (one's gain, another's loss), Rich industrialist, Environment, Adivasi, Mixed goals.
sections.examPointer: CBSE opens with 1 to 3 markers on why notions of development differ, often with a small case of a dam, factory or family; MCQs test the idea of mixed and conflicting goals.

sections.heading: Income and Other Goals
sections.para: Income is important because it buys the goods and services that people need, and average income is the most widely used measure to compare economies. Yet money is not the only thing people want from life. Workers also look at how secure the job is, whether there is paid leave, provident fund and pension, and how they are treated at the workplace. A shopkeeper may prefer respect and the freedom to run his own business over a salaried job with the same earnings. People equally want a pollution free neighbourhood, unadulterated food and protection from disease, which money alone cannot ensure. Women taking up jobs may need safe transport and family support, showing that goals are often mixed and non material. Therefore development is judged not by income alone but by income along with health, education, security and dignity, and public provision becomes essential wherever private money cannot buy these goods.
points: Higher income raises what people can consume, so income remains the most basic development indicator for any household.
People also want equal treatment, freedom, security and respect from others, which income alone cannot deliver.
A job may pay well yet lack permanence, so job security and regular wages must be considered together.
Money cannot buy a pollution free environment or protection from infectious diseases, however rich the buyer may be.
Safe working conditions, paid leave and a pension decide whether a job improves life or merely drains it.
Women may take up jobs only when safe transport and family support exist, proving that goals are often mixed.
A contractor may pay slightly less but treat workers with dignity, and many workers accept such trade offs.
The conclusion for exams is that development must be judged as income plus quality of life, never by income alone.

keyTerms.meaning: A goal linked to income and goods, such as higher wages or a bigger house
Assurance that work and wages will continue, protected against arbitrary dismissal
Overall wellbeing including health, education, environment, security and social respect, not just income
Being treated with respect and equality at work and in society
Clean air, water and surroundings, a collective good that money cannot buy for one person
Balancing one desirable thing against another, such as higher pay against safer work

sections.trick: FSRE train: Freedom, Security, Respect, Environment are the four passengers travelling with Income on the development train.
sections.examPointer: Frequent 3 marker: besides seeking more income, what other things do people desire? Answer with four non material goals and one example; MCQs test which goal money cannot buy.

sections.heading: National Development and the Use of Averages
sections.para: Once we accept that development differs across people, the question arises how to talk about development for a whole nation. National development means improving the living conditions of all the people of a country, and comparisons between countries need a common yardstick. Total income of a country cannot be used because populations differ in size, so the comparison is made through average income or per capita income, which is the total income divided by total population. The World Development Report brought out by the World Bank uses such income data to classify countries. However, an average is only a mathematical summary that conceals how income is actually distributed, and it is silent about health, education and the environment. Hence national development is judged by combining per capita income with human development indicators, so that the growth of a few does not masquerade as the progress of all.
points: National development means improving the living conditions of all the people of a country, not of one region or class.
Countries differ in population size, so their total incomes cannot be compared directly with each other.
Per capita income is the total income of a country divided by its total population, also called average income.
The World Bank publishes the World Development Report, which uses per capita income to classify and compare countries.
An average hides the distribution of income, so two countries with equal averages can have very different inequality.
Averages are silent about health, education and environment, which also decide the quality of life of people.
Income may rise while pollution, disease and insecurity also rise, so income data alone can mislead us about progress.
Therefore comparison always pairs per capita income with health and education indicators to get the full picture.

keyTerms.meaning: Improvement in the living standards of all the people of a country, not just a few individuals
The sum of incomes of all residents of a country, unsuitable for comparison because population sizes differ
Total income divided by total population; also called average income
Annual World Bank report comparing countries on per capita income and related indicators
How income is actually shared among people, which averages conceal
A common standard used for measuring and comparing development

sections.trick: Divide by people (PCI), then check the HEI trio of Health, Education, Income: compare like with like.
sections.examPointer: Expected as a 2 to 3 marker on why total income is not used for comparison; also tested through MCQs on the definition and use of per capita income.

sections.heading: Per Capita Income and World Bank Classification
sections.para: Per capita income is the standard instrument for ranking countries because it is easy to compute and compare. The World Bank classifies economies purely on per capita income. As per the World Development Report 2018, countries with per capita income of US$ 49,300 per annum and above in 2017 are called rich countries, while countries with per capita income of US$ 2,500 or less are called low income countries. India, with a per capita income of US$ 2,450 in 2017, falls in the category of low middle income countries, just below the cut off line. This single number, however, says nothing about how income is shared or how people actually live, which is why the World Bank category of India must always be read with human development data. The classification warns that India remains a poor country by income even while its economy grows, and this is why health and education goals matter alongside income growth.
points: Per capita income is calculated by dividing the total income of a country by its total population.
Countries with per capita income of US$ 49,300 and above in 2017 are called rich countries by the World Bank.
Countries with per capita income of US$ 2,500 or less are classified as low income countries.
India, with a per capita income of US$ 2,450 in 2017, is a low middle income country.
The World Bank classification uses income alone, so it ignores health, education and equality between people.
Rich countries like Norway and the United States also score high on human development indicators.
A quick check: a country earning 500 billion dollars with 50 million people has a per capita income of 10,000 dollars.
Examiners convert these cut off figures into data based MCQs, so memorise all three numbers exactly.

keyTerms.meaning: Average income obtained by dividing national income by population, used for ranking countries
World Bank category for countries with per capita income of US$ 49,300 and above in 2017
World Bank category for countries with per capita income of US$ 2,500 or less
India's World Bank category, with per capita income of US$ 2,450 in 2017
The boundary figure that separates one income category from another
International institution that publishes income based classifications in its World Development Report

sections.trick: Ladder of 2017: above 49,300 is rich, below 2,500 is low income, India at 2,450 sits one rung above low income.
sections.examPointer: One and two markers ask the exact cut offs and India's category; a data based 3 marker may give a country's income and ask its World Bank class.

sections.heading: Comparing States: Kerala versus Haryana
sections.para: Within India, states can be compared exactly like countries, and the Kerala versus Haryana comparison is the textbook proof that income is not the only criterion. Haryana has a much higher per capita income than Kerala, yet Kerala performs far better on human development indicators. The infant mortality rate of Kerala is only 10, while that of Haryana is 30 per thousand live births. The literacy rate of Kerala is 94 percent against 76 percent in Haryana as per the Census of 2011. Even the net attendance ratio at the elementary stage is much higher in Kerala, showing that children there actually sit in classrooms. The reason lies in public provision: Kerala has invested more in schools, primary health centres and mid day meals over decades. Thus a poorer state by income can outperform a richer state wherever government spending reaches the people.
points: Haryana leads Kerala in per capita income, yet trails badly in health and education outcomes.
Infant mortality rate is 10 in Kerala but 30 in Haryana per 1000 live births.
Literacy rate is 94 percent in Kerala against 76 percent in Haryana as per the Census of 2011.
The net attendance ratio at the elementary stage is much higher in Kerala, so children actually sit in classrooms.
Decades of higher public expenditure on healthcare and schooling explain Kerala's superior record in human development.
The comparison proves that money in individual pockets does not automatically convert into health and learning.
Kerala also reports better life expectancy, which underlines the role of a strong public health system.
Whenever explaining this contrast, link the data with public facilities to score the full three or five marks.

keyTerms.meaning: Number of children who die before the age of one year per 1000 live births
Proportion of literate population in the 7 years and above age group
Number of children attending school as a proportion of all children in the same age group
Government spending on services like health, education, water and transport
Improvement in people's health, education and living standards, not income alone
Official decennial count of India's population, the source of literacy data used here

sections.trick: Kerala 10 and 94, Haryana 30 and 76: the smaller the first pair, the bigger the second pair.
sections.examPointer: A table comparing Kerala and Haryana appears in almost every paper as a data based 3 or 5 marker; MCQs demand the exact IMR and literacy figures.

sections.heading: Health and Education Indicators in Detail
sections.para: Development statistics use precise indicators, and students must know their definitions exactly. The infant mortality rate is the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that particular year. The literacy rate measures the proportion of literate population in the 7 years and above age group. The net attendance ratio is the number of children attending school as a proportion of children in the same age group, so it captures actual presence rather than mere enrolment. The Body Mass Index tells whether adults are nourished; it is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the square of height in metres, and a person below 18.5 is undernourished. Life expectancy at birth shows how many years a newborn is expected to live. Together these indicators convert abstract development into measurable numbers that can be compared across states and countries.
points: Infant mortality rate is the number of children dying before the age of one year per 1000 live births.
Literacy rate measures the proportion of literate people in the 7 years and above age group of the population.
Net attendance ratio is the number of children attending school as a proportion of all children in the same age group.
BMI is calculated by dividing a person's weight in kilograms by the square of height in metres.
An adult whose BMI falls below 18.5 is treated as undernourished under this widely used measure.
Life expectancy at birth tells the average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
Sri Lanka reports life expectancy of 77 years against India's 69 years in the HDR 2018 data.
Nepal reports 70, Bangladesh 73 and Pakistan 66, proving that income alone cannot explain health outcomes.

keyTerms.meaning: Infant mortality rate, deaths of children below one year per 1000 live births
Total number of children of age group 6 to 10 attending school as a percentage of children in the same age group
Body Mass Index, weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres, used to check nourishment
A person with BMI below 18.5, indicating inadequate nourishment
Average number of years a newborn is expected to live under current health conditions
A measurable number that stands for a wider aspect of development

sections.trick: ILB: Infant deaths per 1000, Literacy from age 7 plus, BMI below 18.5 signals hunger.
sections.examPointer: Definitions of IMR, net attendance ratio and BMI come as 1 to 2 markers, and calculation questions give data and ask which state or person is undernourished.

sections.heading: Public Facilities: What Money Cannot Buy
sections.para: Money in the pocket cannot buy every good and service that a person needs to live well. Security, freedom, a pollution free environment, unadulterated medicines and protection from infectious diseases are collective goods that no individual can purchase alone. Even rich people cannot buy clean air for their city or stop a disease from spreading in their neighbourhood. This is why governments provide public facilities such as schools, hospitals, safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity, public transport and police protection, which are available to all irrespective of income. Where such facilities are well supplied, as in Kerala, human development improves even with moderate incomes; where they are weak, higher incomes fail to deliver health and learning. Sri Lanka performs better than India on health because of strong public provision. Hence public facilities are not charity but the foundation on which income converts into wellbeing for everyone.
points: Money cannot buy a pollution free environment or protection from infectious diseases for any individual buyer.
Governments provide public facilities like schools, hospitals, safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity and public transport for all.
Kerala's better health status rests on public healthcare and schooling rather than on private spending by families.
Sri Lanka performs better than India in health indicators because of stronger public provision of services.
Even rich people suffer when the air is polluted or epidemics spread, so these goods need collective action.
Unadulterated medicines and safe food require government regulation, which individuals cannot buy for themselves in a market.
Public facilities convert income into wellbeing, especially for the poor who cannot purchase private services.
Exam hook: always link public facilities with the Kerala versus Haryana contrast when explaining human development.

keyTerms.meaning: Essential services like water, health, education, sanitation and transport that the government provides for all
A good that benefits everyone together and cannot be bought by individuals separately, like clean air
Systems for safe disposal of waste and provision of clean surroundings
Government run hospitals, clinics and health programmes open to all citizens
Government rules that force producers to maintain safety and quality standards
Services supplied by individuals or companies for payment, available only to those who can afford them

sections.trick: SHEEP list: Schools, Hospitals, Electricity, Environment, Police and water are what no single wallet can buy.
sections.examPointer: The statement money cannot buy all goods and services is a classic 3 to 5 marker; support it with public facilities and the Kerala versus Haryana evidence.

sections.heading: Human Development Index and the HDR 2018
sections.para: The Human Development Index answers the weakness of income based ranking by combining three dimensions: health, education and income. Health is captured by life expectancy at birth, education by schooling years and literacy, and income by per capita income. The United Nations Development Programme publishes the Human Development Report annually, ranking countries on this composite index. In the HDR 2018, Sri Lanka stands at rank 76 while India stands at 130, even though Sri Lanka's income is much lower; Nepal at 149 and Bangladesh at 136 also show that small, poorer countries can outperform India on people's wellbeing. HDI is considered superior because it treats people, not money, as the measure of development, and it exposes where public spending must go. For exams, remember the three components, India's rank and the Sri Lanka contrast, which together answer almost every HDI question.
points: HDI ranks countries using health, education and income together instead of per capita income alone.
Health is measured by life expectancy, education by years of schooling and literacy, and income by per capita income.
The Human Development Report, which carries the HDI rankings, is published every year by the United Nations Development Programme.
As per the HDR 2018, India's HDI rank is 130 while Sri Lanka's rank is 76.
In the same report, Nepal stands at 149, Bangladesh at 136 and Pakistan at 150.
Sri Lanka's higher rank despite lower income proves that public spending on people matters more than money.
HDI is called a composite index because it combines several indicators into one comparable score.
India's low rank despite medium income signals weak delivery of health and education to ordinary people.

keyTerms.meaning: Human Development Index, a composite ranking of countries on health, education and income
Annual UNDP publication ranking countries on the HDI
United Nations Development Programme, publisher of the HDR
A single score built by combining several different indicators
Expected average lifespan at birth, the health component of HDI
A country's position among all countries on the HDI scale

sections.trick: HEI baby: Health, Education, Income; India 130, Sri Lanka 76, and the gap is the gap in public facilities.
sections.examPointer: Boards ask why HDI is better than per capita income as a 3 marker and test the ranks of India, Sri Lanka and neighbours through MCQs.

sections.heading: Sustainability of Development: The Core Idea
sections.para: Development is not only about the present generation; it must also protect the ability of future generations to meet their needs. Sustainable development is development that takes place without damaging the environment or reducing the resources available for future use. The idea rests on the distinction between renewable and non renewable resources. Renewable resources like groundwater, forests and fish stocks can replenish themselves if used carefully, but they get exhausted when consumption outruns recharge. Non renewable resources like crude oil and minerals have fixed reserves that no present technology can expand, so using them faster cheats future generations. Since scientific methods cannot create unlimited resources, sustainability demands restraint, efficiency and alternative sources. Any development model that raises today's income by exhausting water, soil, forests and fuel is therefore self defeating, and sustainability has become the central test of true development.
points: Sustainable development meets present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Future generations should receive at least as much of the resource base as the present generation inherited.
Renewable resources like groundwater and forests can replenish themselves over time if they are used judiciously.
Non renewable resources like crude oil have fixed reserves and cannot be replenished within a human timescale.
Scientific methods cannot manufacture unlimited water, oil or minerals, so restraint in use is unavoidable.
Overuse today is like borrowing from grandchildren, who will face shortages and higher costs tomorrow.
Sustainability requires efficiency, recycling and a timely switch over to alternative renewable sources of energy like solar power.
Deforestation, falling water tables and rising pollution are warnings that present patterns of growth are unsustainable.

keyTerms.meaning: Development that meets present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet their needs
People yet to be born, whose resource rights sustainability protects
The total stock of natural resources available to a society over time
Natural refilling of a resource like groundwater by rainfall
Complete depletion of a resource due to overuse
Careful and wise use of resources without waste
Substitutes like solar or wind energy that reduce pressure on scarce resources

sections.trick: Borrow from your grandchild: every drop of groundwater and litre of petrol burnt today is a loan that must be repaid now.
sections.examPointer: Define sustainable development and illustrate with one renewable and one non renewable example, usually a 3 or 5 marker; also common as an assertion reason MCQ.

sections.heading: Renewable and Non renewable Resources: Groundwater and Crude Oil
sections.para: The textbook develops sustainability through two examples. Groundwater is a renewable resource: rain refills the water table, and wells can yield water forever if withdrawal stays below recharge. But groundwater is under serious threat in India because overpumping for irrigation and cities has lowered water tables alarmingly; farmers draw more water than rainfall returns, and aquifers deplete. Crude oil is the opposite case: it is a non renewable resource whose reserves are fixed. At the current rate of use, known reserves of crude oil will last only a few decades, and prices will rise as scarcity grows. Both cases lead to the same conclusion: resources must be used carefully, conserved and substituted. Water harvesting, drip irrigation and recharging wells protect the renewable stock, while fuel efficiency and renewable energy reduce pressure on the non renewable stock of oil.
points: Groundwater is renewable because rainfall recharges aquifers, but only if withdrawal stays below the rate of recharge.
Overpumping for irrigation and cities has made falling water tables a serious national problem in India.
When wells run dry, poor families spend more time, money and effort in fetching water for daily needs.
Crude oil is non renewable, so every barrel burnt today permanently reduces the fixed stock left for the future.
Known reserves of crude oil can last only a few decades at the present rate of consumption.
As oil nears exhaustion, its price will rise, hurting net importing countries like India the most.
Water harvesting, drip irrigation and check dams help conserve the renewable stock of groundwater for the future.
Solar energy, wind power and biogas are alternatives that reduce dependence on non renewable crude oil.

keyTerms.meaning: Water stored beneath the earth's surface, a renewable resource refilled by rainfall
The upper level of groundwater below the earth's surface, which falls with overpumping
Drawing groundwater faster than rain can recharge it
Non renewable fossil fuel with fixed reserves used for fuel and petrochemicals
Known quantities of a resource that remain available for extraction
Collecting and storing rainwater to recharge wells and conserve groundwater

sections.trick: G is Green and refillable (Groundwater), O is a One-time gift (Oil): remember GO.
sections.examPointer: Expect a 3 marker asking why groundwater is under threat and how crude oil reserves are limited, with MCQs on which resource is renewable.

sections.heading: Consequences of Overuse and the Path to Sustainability
sections.para: The chapter closes by connecting resource overuse with the quality of life that development was meant to raise. Excessive use of groundwater lowers water tables, forces deeper and costlier wells, and can turn land saline and infertile. Burning more crude oil means more emissions, worsening air quality and climate change, which damage agriculture and health, thus undoing development gains. The textbook also asks students to debate whether a rise in national income is genuine development if pollution, disease and resource scarcity rise alongside it. The path to sustainability includes judicious use of resources, regulation of extraction, investment in public transport and renewable energy, and spreading awareness so that citizens treat water, fuel and forests as shared inheritances. Development, in the end, must be judged by whether it improves wellbeing today without robbing tomorrow, and every citizen shares responsibility for that balance.
points: Overuse of groundwater dries wells, raises costs and can make land saline and infertile over time.
Higher consumption of crude oil means more emissions, worsening air quality and faster climate change.
Climate change damages crops and health, so unsustainable growth destroys the very gains it produces.
A rising national income accompanied by rising pollution and disease is not genuine development for the people.
Judicious use, regulation of extraction and water harvesting together form the practical toolkit of sustainability.
Public transport and renewable energy cut pressure on crude oil and on the environment at the same time.
Awareness campaigns teach citizens to treat water, fuel and forests as shared inheritances of the nation.
The final line for exams: development must improve life today without robbing future generations of their share.

keyTerms.meaning: Falling level of groundwater caused by pumping more than recharge
Gases released by burning fuels, contributing to air pollution and climate change
Long term shift in weather patterns caused mainly by greenhouse gas emissions
Government control over how much of a resource may be extracted or emitted
Fairness between present and future generations in the use of resources
Shared transport like buses and metro that reduces per person fuel use

sections.trick: JURA ladder: Judicious use, Use of alternatives, Regulation, Awareness is the four step climb to sustainability.
sections.examPointer: Applied questions give scenarios like a village with dying wells or a smoggy city and ask for sustainable solutions, usually 3 or 5 marks.

boardQuestions.question: Define per capita income. Why is it used to compare countries?
boardQuestions.answer: Per capita income is the average income of the people of a country, obtained by dividing the total income of the country by its total population. It is used to compare countries because total income cannot be compared directly when populations differ in size.

boardQuestions.question: Why do different persons have different notions of development? Explain with one example.
boardQuestions.answer: People have different life situations, incomes, jobs and aspirations, so each person visualises improvement differently. For example, a landless labourer sees development as regular work, better wages and schooling for children, while an adivasi facing displacement by a dam sees the same project as loss of home and livelihood. Since life situations differ, notions of development also differ, and goals often conflict with one another.

boardQuestions.question: Besides seeking more income, name any four other things that people desire for a good life.
boardQuestions.answer: Besides income, people desire equal treatment, freedom, security and respect from others. They also want job security, safe and clean working conditions, a pollution free environment and good health and education facilities. These non material goals matter because money cannot buy dignity, clean air or protection from disease, so a good life needs income together with these qualities.

boardQuestions.question: Why is total income not used to compare countries? State two limitations of using average income alone.
boardQuestions.answer: Total income cannot be used to compare countries because countries differ in the size of their population; a big country would naturally have a higher total income even if its people are poorer. Hence per capita income, the average income, is used instead. However, average income has two major limitations. First, it hides the distribution of income: a country may have a high average because a few people are extremely rich while the majority remain poor, so the average tells nothing about equality. Second, it ignores non income aspects of wellbeing such as health, education, security and a pollution free environment, which also decide the quality of life. Therefore per capita income must always be read along with indicators like infant mortality rate and literacy rate.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the World Bank classification of countries on the basis of per capita income with the help of data. Where does India stand?
boardQuestions.answer: The World Bank classifies countries purely on the basis of per capita income in its World Development Report. As per the report of 2018, countries with per capita income of US$ 49,300 per annum and above in 2017 are called rich countries, while countries with per capita income of US$ 2,500 or less are called low income countries. India, with a per capita income of US$ 2,450 in 2017, falls in the category of low middle income countries, lying just below the low income cut off. This classification uses income alone and says nothing about health, education or the distribution of income, so it must be combined with human development indicators for a full judgement of development.

boardQuestions.question: Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana but a better record of human development. Explain this statement with data and reasons.
boardQuestions.answer: Development cannot be judged by per capita income alone, and the comparison of Kerala and Haryana proves it. Haryana has a much higher per capita income than Kerala, so judged by income alone Haryana would appear more developed. But the human development indicators tell the opposite story. The infant mortality rate of Kerala is only 10 per 1000 live births, while that of Haryana is 30, which means a child born in Kerala is three times more likely to survive its first year. The literacy rate of Kerala is 94 percent against 76 percent in Haryana as per the Census of 2011, and the net attendance ratio at the elementary stage is also much higher in Kerala, showing that children there actually attend school. The reason for this paradox lies in public facilities. For decades Kerala has spent more and better on public healthcare, primary schools, mid day meals and sanitation, so health and education reach ordinary families even when family incomes are modest. Its public health system ensures immunisation and institutional deliveries, which directly cut infant deaths, and its school system keeps children, including girls, in classrooms, which raises literacy across generations. Haryana, despite its higher income from agriculture and industry, has lagged in providing such public services, so its weaker sections benefit less from the state's prosperity. The lesson is that money in individual pockets cannot automatically buy health and learning; these need public provision. Hence human development, measured by IMR, literacy and net attendance ratio, is a better test of development than income, and Kerala's experience shows that sustained public investment in education and health can produce excellent human development even before incomes catch up.

boardQuestions.question: Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services that you need to live well. Explain this statement with reference to public facilities.
boardQuestions.answer: Money is necessary for a good life, but there are goods and services that money in one's pocket simply cannot buy. Security, freedom, respect and equal treatment are not sold in any market; a rich person cannot purchase the respect of society merely by spending. Similarly, a pollution free environment is a collective good: no individual, however rich, can buy clean air for an entire city or stop an epidemic from spreading in the neighbourhood. Protection from infectious diseases requires public health systems, not private wallets. Unadulterated medicines, safe drinking water for all and uncontaminated food need regulation and public provision, since individuals cannot test every product they consume. This is why governments provide public facilities such as schools, hospitals, safe drinking water, sanitation, electricity, roads and public transport, which are meant for all irrespective of income. The Kerala versus Haryana comparison shows the power of such public facilities: Kerala, with a lower per capita income, records an infant mortality rate of only 10 against Haryana's 30, and a literacy rate of 94 percent against 76 percent, because it has invested more in public health and education. Sri Lanka similarly outranks India in the Human Development Report because of strong public provision in health. The evidence from these examples is that income converts into wellbeing only partly through private purchases; the rest depends on collective goods supplied by the state. Hence development is measured not only by per capita income but also by public facilities and human development indicators. A strategy that ignores public facilities leaves even rich societies unhealthy and uneducated, while one that provides them lifts everyone, including the poorest.

boardQuestions.question: What is sustainable development? Explain with the examples of groundwater and crude oil why sustainable development is essential for India.
boardQuestions.answer: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It rests on the idea that the earth's resources are a shared inheritance, and the present generation is only a trustee which must pass them on intact. Two examples show why sustainability is essential. First, groundwater is a renewable resource because rainfall recharges aquifers, but recharge has a limit. In many parts of India, farmers and cities pump far more water than the rains return, so water tables are falling, wells are running dry, and land is becoming saline and infertile. If this continues, future generations will inherit empty aquifers and face a water crisis that no amount of income can solve quickly. Second, crude oil is a non renewable resource with fixed reserves. At the present rate of consumption, known reserves will last only a few decades, and as scarcity grows, prices will rise sharply, hurting importing countries like India and poor people everywhere. Every barrel burnt today is permanently removed from the stock available tomorrow. These examples show that growth which exhausts resources is self defeating: it raises present income while stealing from the future, and the resulting pollution and climate change damage crops and health, undoing the gains of development. Sustainable development therefore requires judicious use of resources, water harvesting and drip irrigation to conserve groundwater, fuel efficiency and renewable energy such as solar and wind to reduce oil dependence, regulation of extraction, recycling, and public awareness so that citizens treat water, fuel and forests as shared inheritances. Development is genuine only when it improves life today without robbing future generations of their share, and that balance is the essence of sustainability.

boardQuestions.question: Distinguish between renewable and non renewable resources with one example of each.
boardQuestions.answer: Renewable resources are those that can replenish themselves over time if used carefully, so their stock is not permanently reduced by use. Groundwater is a renewable resource because rainfall refills aquifers, though overpumping can still deplete it; forests and fish stocks are similar examples. Non renewable resources are those whose reserves are fixed and which cannot be replenished within a human timescale, so every unit used reduces what remains for the future. Crude oil is a non renewable resource whose known reserves will last only a few decades; coal and minerals are other examples. The distinction matters because renewable resources need careful use below their rate of recharge, while non renewable resources need conservation and substitutes.

boardQuestions.question: Define infant mortality rate, literacy rate and net attendance ratio.
boardQuestions.answer: Infant mortality rate is the number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that particular year. It measures the quality of health services. Literacy rate measures the proportion of literate population in the 7 years and above age group, and reflects the spread of education. Net attendance ratio is the number of children attending school as a proportion of the total number of children in the same age group, so it shows actual attendance rather than mere enrolment. Together these three indicators capture the health and education dimensions of human development.

boardQuestions.question: Study the data: State A has a per capita income of Rs 90,000, an IMR of 32 and a literacy rate of 76 percent. State B has a per capita income of Rs 50,000, an IMR of 10 and a literacy rate of 94 percent. 1) Which state is ahead in income? 2) Which state is ahead in human development? 3) What conclusion do you draw?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) State A is ahead in income, because its per capita income of Rs 90,000 is much higher than State B's Rs 50,000. 2) State B is clearly ahead in human development: its infant mortality rate of 10 is less than one third of State A's 32, meaning far more children survive their first year, and its literacy rate of 94 percent is 18 percentage points above State A's 76 percent. 3) The conclusion is that per capita income alone cannot measure development. State B shows that lower income can coexist with far better health and education when public facilities are strong, so any judgement of development must combine income with human development indicators like IMR and literacy rate.

boardQuestions.question: Case: In a village, farmers have installed deep tube wells and grow water intensive crops. Over the years, the water table has fallen sharply, many wells have dried up, and drinking water has become scarce. 1) Which resource is being overused? 2) Why is this resource called renewable even though it is depleting? 3) Suggest two measures to correct the situation.
boardQuestions.answer: 1) The village is overusing groundwater, drawing it through tube wells faster than nature can replenish it. 2) Groundwater is called renewable because rainfall naturally recharges the water table, so the stock can be restored; it depletes only because withdrawal has crossed the rate of recharge, which shows that renewability depends on judicious use. 3) The village should adopt water harvesting structures like check dams and recharge pits to capture rainwater, and switch from water intensive crops to crops suited to local rainfall, supported by drip irrigation and regulation of tube well use, so that withdrawal once again stays below recharge.

boardQuestions.question: Why is the Human Development Index considered a better measure of development than per capita income?
boardQuestions.answer: Per capita income measures only the average income and hides both inequality and non income aspects of life. The HDI combines health, measured by life expectancy, education, measured by schooling and literacy, and income into one composite index, so it reflects how people actually live. That is why Sri Lanka at rank 76 stands far above India at 130 in the HDR 2018 despite lower income, proving that public spending on health and education can matter more than money alone.
